messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane Faleolo is a 24-year-old Samoan-American pharmacist presenting with a PCL-5 score of 58 following the traumatic death of his younger brother, Sione, approximately fourteen months ago. Sione, then nineteen, was struck and killed by a drunk driver while walking home from a family gathering on a Saturday night. Tane had been the last family member to speak with him, having argued with him briefly at the party over something he now considers trivial. He watched the emergency response from a distance, unable to reach his brother through the crowd before Sione was pronounced dead at the scene. The smell of alcohol had been everywhere that evening — on the guests, on the driver when police restrained him, on the pavement itself, it seemed. The details of that night did not settle into a coherent memory so much as fragment into sensory shards that have never reassembled into a story Tane can tell, even to himself.

In the weeks that followed, Tane found himself unable to construct a clear account of what had happened. When he tries to recall the sequence of events, the narrative collapses — he reaches for it and finds only flashes: Sione's jacket, a stranger's face, the sound of sirens. At other times the memory surfaces without warning and he feels nothing at all, as though he is reviewing footage of someone else's loss. But more often, recall arrives with a wave of guilt so intense it becomes its own kind of punishment, rooted in the conviction that the argument, his failure to walk Sione home, his inaction in those final minutes, made him complicit. These fragmented, guilt-saturated memories do not stay contained. They spill outward, sensitising him to anything that echoes the original night — and so the memories themselves have become a source of new triggers, priming him to detect threat in ordinary experience.

Tane works in a community pharmacy in a busy neighbourhood, and it is there that the triggers have accumulated most visibly. The smell of alcohol on a customer's breath — common enough in a retail setting — can stop him mid-sentence, flooding him with the sensory texture of that night. When he witnesses a customer being rude to a colleague, or sees someone behaving carelessly or dishonestly, the moral wrongness of it lands on him with disproportionate force, pulling him back toward the image of the driver. He has declined every invitation to attend a funeral since Sione's burial, and when a colleague mentioned a cemetery near the pharmacy, he changed the subject and spent the rest of the shift unable to concentrate. His broader sense that his life has been destroyed by what happened, and that he was once a happy person who no longer exists, has made these triggers feel not like isolated reactions but like confirmation — as though the world keeps providing evidence for what he already knows about himself. This appraisal of total ruin amplifies the potency of each trigger, so that situations which might otherwise pass unremarked now carry the weight of proof.

His body has not been quiet through any of this. He is certain, in a way he cannot argue himself out of, that he is permanently altered — that his nervous system now operates on a hair trigger, reacting before thought can intervene. He startles at sounds in the dispensary, keeps himself positioned near exits, and notices his jaw clenched by mid-morning most days. These physical states of hyperarousal are not neutral; they feed directly back into his conviction that his life is broken beyond repair, that a body this vigilant belongs to someone who has lost something permanent. The sense of meaninglessness and destroyed happiness is not merely a mood — it is, for Tane, a conclusion drawn from the evidence his own body keeps presenting.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work last month when a customer smelled strongly of alcohol and Tane had to excuse himself to the back room, where he sat on the floor for several minutes unable to stand. A supervisor noticed. Tane is most afraid that he will never feel like himself again — and most tentatively hoping, though he would not easily say so, that someone might show him he is wrong.
